Year
YēR
n. (rendering Hebrew shānâh and Greek etos, eniautos)
From Old English gēar, common Germanic, cognate with Greek hōra (season, hour) — the root idea being the completed circuit of the seasons and the return of the sun to its place. The Hebrew shānâh comes from a root meaning to repeat or do again, and so names the year by its most obvious property: it comes round. Scripture's year is agricultural and covenantal before it is astronomical — reckoned by seedtime and harvest, and marked out by feasts that God Himself appointed.

Biblical Definition

The year is the great revolving measure of the creature's life, ordained at creation when God set lights in the firmament for signs and for seasons. In Israel the year was not a neutral calendar but a catechism. God reset its beginning at the Exodus — “This month shall be unto you the beginning of months” (Exo 12:2) — so that the nation's reckoning of time itself began at redemption; every subsequent year was counted from the night the blood was on the door. Within the year stood the appointed feasts, and over the years stood the sabbath year, when the land itself rested, and the fiftieth or jubile year, when liberty was proclaimed throughout the land and every man returned unto his possession (Lev 25:10). The year was thus a standing sermon on grace: debts cancelled, inheritances restored, bondage ended, not because the debtor had earned it but because the LORD had appointed a year of release. Isaiah gathers all of it into a Messianic title, “the acceptable year of the LORD” (Isa 61:2), which the Lord Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth and applied to Himself. Set against this is the brevity of the creature's own tale of years — threescore years and ten, and if by strength fourscore, yet their strength is labour and sorrow (Psa 90:10). The year both measures our life and outlasts it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The period of the earth's revolution, reckoned in Scripture by seedtime and harvest and by the feasts God appointed; the covenantal measure of Israel's life, containing the sabbath year and the jubile, and the standing measure of the brevity of man.

YEAR, n. 1. The period of time in which the sun returns to the same point in the ecliptic, or the period in which the earth completes its revolution about the sun.

2. In Scripture, the year is reckoned from the month Abib or Nisan, which God appointed to be the beginning of months at the departure from Egypt. The civil year began in Tisri, the seventh month; the sacred year at the Passover.

3. Years, in the plural, denotes age, or old age. He is a man in years. The days of the years of my pilgrimage. Genesis 47.

4. Sabbatical year; the seventh year, in which the Israelites were commanded to let the land rest, neither sowing the field nor pruning the vineyard, the LORD undertaking to command his blessing on the sixth.

5. Year of jubile; the fiftieth year, in which liberty was proclaimed to all the inhabitants of the land, servants released, and possessions reverting to their ancient owners. Levit. 25.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 25:10 — "And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family."

Isaiah 61:2 — "To proclaim the acceptable year of the LORD, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all that mourn;"

Psalm 90:10 — "The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away."

Deuteronomy 11:12 — "A land which the LORD thy God careth for: the eyes of the LORD thy God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year even unto the end of the year."

Modern Corruption

The modern year is a unit of production and self-improvement, measured by what a man got done in it; the biblical year is a unit of accountability and release, measured by what God appointed in it.

expand to see more

The calendar is never doctrinally neutral, and the reordering of the year is one of the quietest ways a people is discipled. Israel's year began at redemption and was punctuated by feasts commemorating God's acts; the commercial year now begins at a fiscal quarter and is punctuated by seasons of purchase. What is lost is not sentiment but instruction. A year framed by Passover and atonement teaches a nation that it exists by deliverance and needs a covering for sin; a year framed by resolutions in January teaches that a man is his own project and the deficiency is one of discipline. The remedy is not a scheme of new holy days — the regulative principle governs the church's worship, and the Lord's Day is the weekly appointment God has actually given — but a household reckoning of the year under providence rather than under productivity.

The jubile is the point at which the modern instinct most plainly fails. Lev 25 makes release a matter of divine appointment rather than of the creditor's generosity or the debtor's merit: at the sound of the trumpet the land returned, because the land was the LORD's and the men were His servants, not their own. That is a picture of the gospel, and it cannot be reduced to a programme of economic policy without losing precisely what it teaches. The acceptable year of the LORD which Christ proclaimed is not an improved arrangement of debts; it is the liberty of captives whose ransom another has paid in full.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shānâh names the year from a root meaning to repeat — the returning circuit. Greek etos is the ordinary year of reckoning; eniautos tends toward the year as a completed cycle, and is the word used of the acceptable year and of the high priest's yearly entrance.

expand to see more

Hebrew shānâh (H8141) — year; from shānâh (H8138), to repeat or do again, naming the year by its recurrence. Some 875 occurrences.

Hebrew yōbēl (H3104) — jubile; properly the blast of a ram's horn, and so the year announced by that blast, the fiftieth.

Hebrew shēmīttâh — the release of the seventh year (Deu 15:1), from a root meaning to let drop or let fall; the debt is not collected but let go.

Greek etos (G2094) — year, the plain unit of reckoning; used of the woman with an issue of blood twelve years, and of the thousand years of Rev 20.

Greek eniautos (G1763) — a year viewed as a completed cycle; used in Luk 4:19 of the acceptable year of the Lord and in Heb 9:7 of the yearly Day of Atonement.

Usage

"Of the covenantal calendar: the beginning of months at the Exodus (Exo 12:2), the three yearly feasts (Exo 23:14), the sabbath year and the jubile (Lev 25)."

"Of age and the span of life: the days of the years of a pilgrimage (Gen 47:9); threescore years and ten (Psa 90:10); Methuselah's nine hundred sixty and nine years (Gen 5:27)."

"Of the Messianic proclamation: the acceptable year of the LORD (Isa 61:2), read by Christ at Nazareth and declared fulfilled in the hearing of the synagogue."
